title: Critical Thinking: Reason Better, Decide Better
description: An original two-hour adult learning course based on Richard Paul and Linda Elder. Analyze reasoning, apply intellectual standards, practice intellectual traits, and defend a decision with evidence.

slides.title: Critical Thinking
slides.notes: FACILITATOR: Open with a recent decision you revised. Ask what evidence changed your mind. Explain that questioning a conclusion is a professional skill. This course teaches the framework, then applies it to fictional service and technology decisions. Invite participants to use the companion workbook or paper. Do not treat the quiz as an externally verified qualification.

objects.name: 1. Map the purpose, question, information, inferences, assumption
objects.text:
1. Map the purpose, question, information, inferences, assumptions, concepts, viewpoints, and implications of a decision.
2. Improve a claim using intellectual standards.
3. Separate recorded information from interpretations and assumptions.
4. Question your own position fairly and revise it when justified.
5. Write a defensible decision brief with limits and a review trigger.

slides.title: A repeatable reasoning practice
slides.notes: FACILITATOR: Ask learners to explain the difference between naming an assumption and judging its quality. Example: The tool caused delays is an inference. Accuracy asks which records support it. Humility helps acknowledge that the explanation is still uncertain. Avoid treating the three framework components as separate memorization lists.

objects.name: The Foundation for Critical Thinking provides original resources
objects.text:
The Foundation for Critical Thinking provides original resources on the elements of reasoning, intellectual standards, intellectual traits, and the distinction between inferences and assumptions.

This course uses original fictional cases and activities to practice those ideas. Continue using the framework on your own reasoning; one short course does not establish mastery of intellectual character.

capstoneRubric: State the outcome and a bounded question that guides the recommendation.
Use case figures correctly; address duplicates and comparison limits.
Separate recorded observations from causal and predictive conclusions.
Identify two important assumptions and useful checks.
Apply three named standards to improve specific parts of the reasoning.
Represent a competing perspective fairly and apply consistent evidence rules.
Compare benefits, risks, stakeholder effects, and a proportionate action.
Acknowledge limits and specify evidence or a review trigger that would change the decision.
